r: MTR 1400 teaches the physical basis of weather and climate — heat and energy transfer, pressure, wind, cloud formation, and atmospheric stability — that underlies later forecasting, storm analysis, and climate-impact reasoning across the meteorology curriculum. Present-day AI systems can summarize these processes fluently, but observed-usage data from the Anthropic Economic Index shows current deployment concentrates in computer-and-mathematical and writing tasks rather than structured physical-science instruction, and task-exposure research finds science and critical-thinking skills negatively associated with exposure. A beginning student still needs the course's guided reasoning about energy balance and stability to interpret model output critically rather than accept plausible-sounding explanations. The binding constraint is institutional: this is a GT-Pathways Natural and Physical Sciences course, a statutory gen-ed transfer requirement independent of AI capability, which anchors near-term demand regardless of how well AI can explain atmospheric physics.

By 2031, AI tutoring tools will likely generate fluent explanations of concepts like adiabatic cooling and geostrophic wind, and diffusion research suggests such tools will see broader classroom adoption, though real-world uptake has historically lagged raw capability. The course increasingly functions as load-bearing scaffolding: Weather Discussion, Climatology, and Climate Change Science all list MTR 1400 as a prerequisite, so even as AI narrows the instrumental need for lecture-delivered content, the sequencing role keeps the course structurally necessary for the major. GT-Pathways designation continues anchoring transfer-credit demand independent of AI capability. Verification burden stays real: students must still confirm AI-generated atmospheric explanations are accurate, echoing the jagged-frontier finding that misplaced trust in AI outputs outside their demonstrated competence produces measurable accuracy costs. Confidence in this trajectory is moderate given how quickly underlying model capability is moving.

Ten years out, capability trends — AI task-time horizons compounding on a several-month doubling cycle per METR/Epoch tracking — make it plausible that much of MTR 1400's expository content could be delivered competently by AI systems, even as macro-level productivity effects remain comparatively modest per Acemoglu-style estimates. Even so, the course's dual role as a GT-Pathways transfer requirement and as the entry prerequisite for the department's upper-division sequence caps the instrumental-need reduction at Medium rather than High: institutions do not retire mandated gen-ed science requirements on the strength of AI capability alone, and program sequencing still requires a structured on-ramp into the discipline's vocabulary and reasoning habits. Whether transfer-credit policy or prerequisite structures themselves shift by 2036 is genuinely uncertain, so this rating should be read as directional rather than a confident point prediction.
MTR 1400.d: This course introduces the fundamental physical processes in the atmosphere-heat and energy, temperature, pressure, wind, clouds, precipitation, and stability. These concepts provide the basis for understanding weather systems, such as thunderstorms, tornadoes, and hurricanes. These processes are also applied to climatic patterns and the impacts of human activity on weather and climate, such as air pollution and climate change. An optional 1- credit lab course, MTR 2020 Weather and Climate Lab for Scientists, is available for students interested in additional experience in the measurement and analysis of atmospheric data, and is required for some science programs.

r: MTR 1600 applies Earth-systems and atmospheric science to regional impacts of global warming, then layers in societal, cultural, and economic analysis of mitigation and adaptation across fossil-fuel-rich, high-emission, and vulnerable regions. This blends scientific reasoning with synthesis and writing tasks, and observed-usage data shows writing and office-style work prominent in current AI deployment, meaning some report-style synthesis is already assistable. Still, task-exposure research finds science and critical-thinking skills negatively associated with exposure, and the course's core work — connecting physical climate mechanisms to region-specific social and economic consequences — requires judgment AI cannot yet reliably supply unsupervised. The binding constraint is institutional: MTR 1600 carries GT-Pathways Natural and Physical Sciences designation plus a Global Diversity gen-ed label, a statutory transfer requirement that anchors demand independent of AI's growing fluency with climate synthesis writing.

By 2031, AI systems will likely handle much of the descriptive synthesis this course currently teaches — summarizing regional climate impacts, mitigation strategies, and interdependence among emitting and vulnerable regions — since professional-writing productivity research already shows substantial time savings with quality gains on this kind of task. Diffusion remains uneven, however, with only a minority of firms and, by extension, instructional contexts fully integrating such tools, so adoption in gen-ed science instruction likely lags the technical ceiling. GT-Pathways and Global Diversity designations continue to anchor the course as a transfer requirement regardless of how AI-capable the subject matter becomes. The interpretive core — weighing which regional impacts and equity tradeoffs matter most — still benefits from instructor-guided reasoning that current AI cannot fully substitute for. Confidence in the pace of this shift is moderate.

By 2036, capability trends suggest AI could plausibly perform most of the descriptive climate-impact synthesis this course currently develops, compounding on several-month task-horizon doubling and continuing compute growth. Yet the GT-Pathways Natural and Physical Sciences and Global Diversity designations are gen-ed transfer mandates that Colorado institutions do not retract based on subject-matter automatability, so the course's institutional lock-in caps the instrumental-need reduction at Medium even under an optimistic capability trajectory. Macro productivity effects from AI remain modest by most current estimates, suggesting slow diffusion into curricular policy even where technical capability runs far ahead. Whether the course's interdisciplinary framing — connecting atmospheric science to global equity questions — retains value that resists full AI substitution is a judgment this analysis cannot make with confidence at a ten-year horizon; the rating here is deliberately hedged rather than a firm prediction.
MTR 1600.d: This course presents the science behind global climate change from an Earth systems and atmospheric science perspective. These concepts then provide the basis to explore the effect of global warming on regions throughout the world. This leads to the analysis of the observed and predicted impacts of climate change on these regions; the effect of these changes on each region's society, culture, and economy; and the efforts of these regions to mitigate or adapt to climate change. The interdependence of all nations will be discussed in regards to fossil fuel-rich regions, regions responsible for greenhouse gas emissions, and regions most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change.

r: This lab course has students take actual surface and upper-air measurements, produce hand-drawn thermodynamic diagrams and weather charts, decode weather codes, and only then move to computer analysis and display software. The manual, hands-on component — physically constructing charts and interpreting raw instrument output before trusting software — is precisely the kind of embodied, psychomotor task that task-exposure research and observed manual-work patterns classify as low-exposure regardless of how capable AI becomes at downstream data analysis. AI can already generate polished visualizations from clean meteorological datasets, but it cannot substitute for the trained-by-hand skill of producing and cross-checking a surface analysis chart, which is the course's central competency. No general-studies designation constrains this course, but the embodied lab format itself is the protective factor here.

By 2031, AI-assisted analysis and display tools will likely handle more of the downstream data visualization this course introduces, and diffusion of such tools into introductory science labs will probably grow, though unevenly across institutions per adoption research. The hand-analysis component, however — constructing thermodynamic diagrams and surface charts manually to internalize how raw observations relate to derived atmospheric fields — remains a psychomotor and pedagogical exercise that AI performing the same task for a student would not replace, since the course's purpose is skill-building rather than output production. The jagged-frontier finding that AI users outside a task's true competence boundary make more errors while trusting outputs more is directly relevant: students still need the manual-analysis grounding to catch software errors later. This assessment carries the usual caveats about lab-course redesign decisions at the institutional level.

A decade out, it is plausible that automated data-analysis and display software further reduces the instrumental value of manually producing charts and diagrams, but the embodied, applied nature of this lab — physically working with instruments, hand-analysis techniques, and observation data before any software mediates the process — keeps its foundational skill-building role largely intact. Capability trends point toward AI systems that can generate any given chart or diagram on request, yet the course exists to teach the underlying judgment for reading raw data correctly, a skill that transfers into instrument-use and quality-control contexts AI cannot embody. Predicting exactly how lab pedagogy evolves that far out is speculative; this rating assumes the applied-measurement core persists as a requirement even as surrounding software tooling continues to automate faster.
MTR 2020.d: Students are introduced to the basic measurements, calculations and analysis made in the study of atmospheric science. Meteorological lab work in the course includes surface and upper-air charts, thermodynamic diagrams, weather codes, and weather imagery. Students analyze and display weather data in multiple formats, using both traditional hand analysis and using computer analysis and display software.

r: This service-learning course requires students to interact directly with local communities, attend neighborhood meetings, and co-develop climate action plans grounded in real, place-specific carbon and water-usage data. The statistical and qualitative analysis of reduction strategies is desk work AI already assists with reasonably well, consistent with observed automation-leaning usage patterns in the Anthropic Economic Index for consumer tasks. But the course's defining activity — building trust with a specific neighborhood, running participatory meetings, and negotiating community priorities in real time — is embodied, interpersonal work that current AI cannot perform. Required in-person participation in neighborhood meetings is the binding constraint here, not an institutional mandate but a structural feature of the course design itself, and it keeps the instrumental need for a present, engaged student high regardless of how good AI gets at the analytical backend.

By 2031, AI tools will likely handle a larger share of the carbon- and water-usage analysis this course requires — modeling reduction scenarios, drafting portions of climate action plans, and synthesizing prior community input — since real-deliverable benchmarks show AI approaching, though not yet matching, expert-level performance on this kind of applied analytical work. The service-learning core, however, still requires a student physically present at neighborhood meetings, building the relationships that make a community climate plan legitimate and usable; that interpersonal, place-based work resists substitution regardless of analytical capability elsewhere in the course. Community engagement pedagogy itself may evolve to incorporate AI-supported drafting tools, but the requirement for direct human interaction with residents is a structural design choice unlikely to be automated away. This projection carries real uncertainty about how community-engagement course design responds to available tools.

Ten years out, the analytical portions of this course — data synthesis, scenario modeling, drafting — could plausibly be substantially AI-assisted, nudging the overall instrumental-need reduction from Low toward Medium as capability compounds on the multi-month task-horizon doubling trend. The service-learning requirement for direct neighborhood engagement is the more durable constraint: real-time trust-building with community stakeholders is exactly the kind of embodied, socially situated work that task-exposure research associates with persistently low exposure, even under aggressive capability assumptions. Macro-level productivity effects from AI remain modest by most estimates, suggesting community-engagement pedagogy changes slowly even where backend analysis becomes highly capable. Whether service-learning requirements themselves get redesigned around AI-assisted planning tools by 2036 is not something this analysis can predict with confidence, and the Medium rating here reflects that residual uncertainty rather than a firm forecast.
MTR 2050.d: Students interact with local communities to develop climate action plans. To prepare for this, students examine neighborhood carbon and water usage, including statistical and qualitative analysis of different reduction strategies and technologies. This course is service learning based and participation in neighborhood meetings is required.

r: This course surveys the instruments used in operational and research meteorology — surface and upper-air sensors, radar, satellites — and its lab component has students calibrate and maintain physical instruments, then analyze and interpret the observations those instruments produce. The calibration and maintenance work is physical, psychomotor, hands-on labor with real equipment, squarely in the category task-exposure research and observed manual-work patterns classify as low-exposure regardless of overall AI progress. AI can already explain sensor theory and operating principles competently, and can help interpret resulting data, but it cannot calibrate a physical anemometer or diagnose a malfunctioning radar unit remotely without a trained person present. This embodied constraint, not any general-studies mandate, is what keeps the instrumental need for the course high today.

By 2031, AI will likely be even more capable at explaining instrument theory, error sources, and operating principles, and diffusion research suggests broader use of such explanatory tools in technical instruction generally, though adoption in specialized instrument labs will likely trail behind office-context adoption. The core constraint remains physical: calibrating, maintaining, and troubleshooting surface- and upper-air sensor systems, radar, and satellite receiving equipment requires hands-on interaction with hardware that AI cannot yet perform remotely or autonomously. The jagged-frontier finding — that AI users trust outputs more than warranted outside a system's true competence — is particularly relevant to instrument calibration, where an uncaught sensor error propagates into every downstream forecast. This trajectory assumes no near-term breakthrough in physically embodied AI systems capable of servicing meteorological instrumentation, which is a reasonable but not certain assumption.

A decade out, robotics and embodied-AI progress could in principle narrow the gap on some instrument-maintenance tasks, but current capability trends are concentrated in digital, language-mediated work rather than physical equipment servicing, and this course's core content — hands-on calibration, maintenance, and fault diagnosis of sensor and radar systems — sits outside that trajectory. The analysis and interpretation component layered on top of the hardware work could see more AI assistance by 2036, but it does not change the course's foundational reliance on physically capable, trained technicians. Predicting the pace of embodied-AI progress specifically is considerably more uncertain than predicting progress in purely digital domains, so this Low rating is held with appropriate caution about robotics timelines rather than confidence about digital-task automation alone.
MTR 2410.d: This course provides a survey of the instruments and instrument systems used in operational and research meteorology. The theory of instrument measurement and error, operating principles, and method of operation of surface- and upper-air sensors, as well as radar and satellites, will be presented. The lab component of the course will involve the theory, use, calibration, and maintenance of instruments and the analysis and interpretation of the observations.

r: Weather Discussion has students interpret radar data, satellite animations, weather observations, and forecasting-model output to produce weather forecasts in a weekly interactive format — precisely the kind of numerical-model-interpretation task where AI weather systems have already demonstrated strong real-world performance. Real-deliverable benchmarking shows leading models reaching close to, though still short of, expert-level results on applied occupational tasks of this kind, and observed-usage data confirms computer-and-mathematical work is the largest category of current AI deployment. Students today can already lean on AI tools to help interpret model guidance, narrowing but not eliminating the course's value, since synthesizing competing model outputs into a specific, defensible forecast still benefits from an instructor-guided discussion format that catches reasoning errors before they compound into a bad forecast.

By 2031, AI weather-interpretation tools will likely be substantially more capable at synthesizing radar, satellite, and model-ensemble data into forecast products, consistent with capability-trend research showing AI task-time horizons compounding on a several-month doubling cycle. The interactive discussion format this course uses — students defending forecast reasoning against classmates and an instructor — increasingly functions as a check on AI-generated guidance rather than a substitute for independent human forecasting skill, since verification burden rises as models get more capable and more heavily relied upon: someone still needs domain knowledge to catch a plausible-sounding but wrong AI forecast, echoing the jagged-frontier finding on miscalibrated trust. This pushes the rating to High even at this horizon, though the confidence behind it is only moderate given how quickly numerical weather-model capability specifically has been advancing.

By 2036, it is plausible that AI systems handle the great majority of routine forecast synthesis this course teaches, given how far numerical-weather AI capability has already progressed relative to other domains and how fast task-time horizons are compounding under current trends. The course's discussion-and-defense format could persist less as forecasting training and more as a verification-and-judgment exercise for evaluating AI-generated guidance, but that shift does not change the instrumental-need assessment, since the underlying work — producing and defending a specific forecast — is what AI increasingly performs directly. This is a genuinely fast-moving subdomain, and predicting the exact state of human-forecaster necessity a decade out is speculative; the High rating here should be read as a directional judgment under real uncertainty about how forecasting workflows and verification norms evolve.
MTR 3000.d: In this interactive weather discussion course, students will participate in weekly weather discussions on recent, present, and future weather. Students will become familiar with weather patterns and learn to create weather forecasts through the discussion and interpretation of radar data, satellite animations, weather observations, and forecasting models.

r: This course teaches Python specifically for loading, manipulating, analyzing, and visualizing meteorological data — a domain-flavored version of general-purpose programming instruction. Task-exposure research finds programming among the skills most strongly and positively associated with AI exposure, and productivity research on AI coding assistants shows substantial task-speed gains already realized in practice, with observed-usage data confirming computer-and-mathematical work as the largest current category of AI deployment. Students today can already generate, debug, and explain meteorological data-processing scripts with AI assistance at a level that directly substitutes for much of what this course teaches procedurally. The instrumental need for structured human instruction in basic Python syntax and workflow is already substantially reduced, even though domain-specific data-format handling and visualization choices still benefit from course-provided context.

By 2031, AI coding assistance will likely be even more deeply integrated into scientific-computing workflows, and the productivity gains already documented for general programming assistance should extend further into meteorology-specific applications like loading NetCDF files, building map-based visualizations, or automating batch analysis of atmospheric datasets. Verification burden remains a real, if moderate, constraint — silently wrong scientific code can propagate errors into research or operational products — but this affects how the skill is exercised more than whether AI can perform the underlying programming tasks competently. The course's coverage of universal programming concepts alongside meteorology-specific applications is precisely the kind of digitally mediated, non-embodied work capability-trend research suggests advances fastest. Confidence here is high given how directly programming instruction maps onto documented AI coding strengths, though the exact pace of further gains carries some uncertainty.

A decade out, it is difficult to construct a scenario, given current capability trajectories in code generation and scientific-computing assistance, where AI does not perform the great majority of the data-loading, manipulation, and visualization tasks this course teaches as procedural skills. Compute and capability continue compounding on documented trends, and programming remains one of the domains where task-exposure research shows the strongest positive association with AI substitution. What likely persists is the need for domain judgment — knowing which meteorological variables matter, how to validate a visualization's scientific accuracy, what analysis a given atmospheric question calls for — but that shifts the course's value toward domain framing rather than programming instruction itself. This is a fast-moving area and a ten-year projection carries real uncertainty about exact tooling, but the directional confidence in continued high automatability is strong.
MTR 3040.n: September 2026 evidence update. Task automatability (F1) raised at 24 months from 4 to 5. Introductory Python course for loading, manipulating, and plotting meteorological data, which is routine scripting. Stanford's August 2026 payroll update places software developers and computer programmers in the most AI-exposed occupations, where employment of 22-to-25-year-olds is 19% below trend, mainly through reduced hiring; the Bureau of Labor Statistics' 2025-35 projections put computer programmers at -7.3%. Both are descriptive signals, not proof that AI caused the decline. No rating changed, because an existing cap already binds.
MTR 3040.d: Students are introduced to the computer programming language Python, the modern language used in the atmospheric sciences. The course content focuses on specific applications to meteorology, including basic universal programming concepts. Students learn to load, manipulate, and analyze meteorological data of various formats, and visualize it through graphs and maps. Students become familiar with a variety of python tools for these tasks while practicing these concepts in a lab setting.

r: Air Pollution covers pollutant sources and sinks, regional and global pollution problems, monitoring and sampling techniques, regulatory control, meteorological influences on dispersion, and indoor air quality — a mix of applied science and regulatory-compliance analysis. The regulatory and compliance-evaluation components are exactly the kind of structured-document work where observed AI usage skews toward automation rather than augmentation in consumer contexts, and AI can already draft competent summaries of pollution-control regulations and dispersion modeling concepts. The monitoring and sampling techniques portion retains a modest field component that tempers full automatability today. Given the blend, the course sits at Medium: meaningful analytical work is already AI-assistable, but synthesizing meteorological influences with regulatory frameworks into a coherent compliance judgment still benefits from structured instruction rather than ad hoc AI queries.

By 2031, AI systems will likely handle a larger share of the regulatory-compliance analysis and pollution-dispersion modeling this course covers, since real-deliverable benchmarking shows AI capability on applied analytical tasks continuing to close the gap with expert human output, even though actual firm-level adoption of such tools remains uneven per diffusion research. The meteorological-influences component — connecting atmospheric conditions to pollutant transport and concentration — is conceptually similar to forecasting-adjacent reasoning that AI handles increasingly well. What likely persists longer is judgment about which regulatory standard applies to a specific, ambiguous real-world scenario, since compliance determinations carry real consequences that raise verification burden. This pushes the rating to High at this horizon, with moderate confidence given uncertainty about how quickly environmental-compliance-specific AI tools mature relative to general-purpose capability.

By 2036, capability trends suggest AI could plausibly perform most of the descriptive and analytical work this course currently teaches — characterizing pollution sources, modeling meteorological dispersion, and mapping monitoring data against regulatory thresholds — as task-time horizons continue compounding under documented trends. Diffusion into environmental-compliance workflows specifically will likely lag the technical ceiling, since adoption research shows only a minority of firms using AI systems broadly even as capability advances faster. No accreditation or licensure mandate anchors this specific course, so the primary residual constraint is verification burden: compliance judgments with legal and public-health consequences still call for accountable human review. Predicting the exact state of environmental-regulatory AI tooling a decade out is speculative, and this High rating should be read as directional rather than a confident point forecast.
MTR 3100.d: This course examines the causes and control of air pollution. Topics include pollutant sources and sinks, regional and global-scale pollution problems, monitoring and sampling techniques, regulatory control, meteorological influences, and indoor air quality.

r: Climatology examines the characteristics, distribution, and physical and dynamic causes of global and regional climate, along with spatial and temporal distributions of climate elements, paleoclimatology, and climate-model projections. This is fully digital, desk-based analytical work — reading model output, characterizing spatial patterns, synthesizing paleoclimate proxy data — that maps closely onto the computer-and-mathematical category observed usage data identifies as the largest current segment of AI deployment. AI tools today can already summarize climate model projections and describe regional climate distributions competently. Task-exposure research's finding that science and critical-thinking skills correlate negatively with exposure provides some counterweight, since synthesizing which physical mechanisms explain a given regional climate pattern still requires disciplinary judgment current tools apply inconsistently, keeping this course at Medium rather than higher in the near term.

By 2031, AI systems will likely be substantially more capable at interpreting climate-model projections, characterizing spatial and temporal distributions of climate variables, and synthesizing paleoclimatology evidence, consistent with capability-trend research showing AI task-time horizons compounding on a multi-month doubling cycle. No general-studies designation or accreditation mandate anchors this specific upper-division course, so its instrumental necessity tracks capability more directly than gen-ed courses do. The physical-and-dynamic-mechanisms component of the course — explaining why a given climate pattern arises rather than merely describing it — is the piece most likely to retain some instructor-guided value, but even that increasingly overlaps with what capable AI systems can articulate. This pushes the rating to High at this horizon, held with moderate confidence given the pace of underlying capability change.

A decade out, it is plausible that AI performs most of the descriptive and even much of the explanatory work this course currently teaches — characterizing climate distributions, working through paleoclimate evidence, and interpreting model projections — as capability and compute continue compounding on documented trends. Without an institutional lock-in comparable to a GT-Pathways designation or licensure mandate, this upper-division course's instrumental need tracks capability growth closely rather than being cushioned by a fixed transfer requirement. The main residual argument for continued human involvement is verification: climate-model interpretation carries real consequences for downstream policy and research conclusions, and misplaced trust in AI output outside its true competence is a documented failure mode. Given how fast this specific analytical domain has been advancing, the ten-year horizon carries real uncertainty, and this High rating is offered as a directional judgment rather than a firm prediction.
MTR 3330.d: Climatology examines the characteristics, distribution, and causes of global and regional climate. Physical and dynamic mechanisms of climate are emphasized. The course also explores the spatial and temporal distributions of the main climate elements. Climate change topics include paleoclimatology, observed shifts in climate, climate model projections, and potential impacts of global warming.

r: Climate Change Science examines the physical mechanisms of climate change through an integrative Earth-systems lens — energy movement through the Earth system, atmospheric and oceanic circulation, hydrologic and carbon cycles — and applies that understanding to interpreting climate-model projections, climate sensitivity, and sources of uncertainty. This is digital, analytical, desk-based work well within the reach of current AI systems for descriptive synthesis, though real-deliverable benchmarking shows even the best models still fall short of consistent expert-level performance on complex applied scientific reasoning. The course's emphasis on uncertainty sources and climate sensitivity requires holding multiple lines of physical evidence together, a task where task-exposure research's science-and-critical-thinking protection still applies today. This combination places the course at Medium: substantial AI assistance is already possible, but full substitution for the integrative reasoning is not yet reliable.

By 2031, AI systems will likely handle a larger share of the descriptive and comparative work in this course — summarizing carbon-cycle dynamics, comparing climate-model projections, characterizing sources of uncertainty — since capability-trend research shows AI task-time horizons compounding on a several-month doubling cycle. No GT-Pathways designation or accreditation mandate protects this upper-division elective, so its instrumental necessity should track capability growth more directly than gen-ed courses with fixed transfer requirements. The integrative Earth-systems reasoning that connects energy, ocean-atmosphere circulation, and biogeochemical cycles into coherent explanations of climate sensitivity is the more durable piece, but even that increasingly overlaps with what advanced models can articulate credibly. This pushes the rating to High at this horizon, held with moderate confidence given real uncertainty about how fast integrative-reasoning capability specifically improves.

By 2036, it is plausible AI performs most of the descriptive and integrative synthesis this course teaches, as capability and compute continue compounding under documented trends, even though macro-level productivity effects from AI remain comparatively modest by most current estimates, implying slower real-world diffusion than raw capability would suggest. Without institutional lock-in, this course's instrumental necessity is not cushioned the way a mandated gen-ed science requirement would be, so a high rating at this horizon is defensible. The strongest counterargument is that climate-sensitivity and uncertainty-quantification reasoning sits close to genuine scientific research, where verification burden and the cost of confidently wrong conclusions stay high regardless of AI fluency. Given how much scientific and institutional change could occur over a decade, this rating is held with appropriate hedging rather than confidence in a specific outcome.
MTR 3340.d: This course examines the physical mechanisms of climate change through an integrative earth systems science lens. These processes explain many of the observed changes within the atmosphere, hydrosphere, cryosphere, biosphere, and lithosphere of the planet. Aspects of dynamic climate change include movement of energy through the Earth system, atmospheric and oceanic circulation, and hydrologic and carbon cycles. This understanding is applied to interpreting climate model projections, with keen attention to climate sensitivity, time scales of changes, and sources of uncertainty in climate prediction. An understanding of the physical processes driving climate models facilitates an examination of climate change impacts on natural and societal systems.

r: Synoptic Meteorology develops a descriptive command of mid-latitude weather systems: reading airmasses, fronts, jet-stream configuration, and the general circulation, then applying that framework to cyclone and anticyclone development, with elementary quasi-geostrophic forecasting introduced. These tasks map to analyzing meteorological data and interpreting synoptic information for downstream users, activities where task-exposure research finds a mixed profile: pattern recognition is increasingly automatable, while critical scientific reasoning about atmospheric causation stays comparatively protected. No general-studies designation locks this course into a transfer core, so the binding constraint is instead its role as prerequisite substrate feeding Weather Analysis Techniques. At 24 months, observed-usage data confirms quantitative-analytical work is a growing but still largely augmentative AI use case; the instrumental need to build synoptic reasoning firsthand remains intact, and the rating sits at Medium given the already-exposed descriptive-classification content.

By 2031, capability-trend evidence on rapid task-time-horizon growth points to AI systems handling much of the descriptive synoptic-pattern classification this course teaches: recognizing frontal structures, jet placement, and cyclogenesis signatures from data with declining need for a human to work the physics by hand. The elementary forecasting component sits inside the more-exposed quantitative-analytical band that task-exposure research identifies. Verification burden is only moderate here, since this is an introductory framework rather than operational warning issuance, and embodiment is minimal, so protective dampening is limited. The course's prerequisite role for Weather Analysis Techniques provides some structural durability but does not cap the rating outright at this horizon. The instrumental case shifts toward High: AI increasingly performs the descriptive classification even as students still need conceptual grounding to interpret and direct it.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems performing synoptic classification, frontal analysis, and cyclone diagnosis with high reliability, consistent with capability-trend projections of rapidly compounding task-horizon length. Task-exposure research's negative association between science reasoning and exposure offers some counterweight, but this course's content, descriptive pattern recognition applied to weather systems, sits closer to the analytical tasks that research flags as increasingly automatable than to the deepest theoretical reasoning found elsewhere in the major. With no institutional lock-in and only moderate verification demands, little structurally protects the course from continued erosion. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much operational synoptic interpretation remains human-directed versus fully automated by 2036; the central case favors substantial AI capability, though diffusion evidence shows adoption could still lag the technical frontier considerably.
MTR 3400.d: This course presents a descriptive approach to the structure and behavior of mid-latitude, synoptic-scale weather systems. Primary topics include the physics of synoptic-scale air motion, the role of synoptic weather systems in the general circulation, jet streams, airmasses, fronts, and the application of these to cyclones and anticyclones. Elementary quasi-geostrophic theory and weather forecasting are introduced.

r: Weather Analysis Techniques teaches hand analysis of surface and upper-air maps, thermodynamic diagrams, meso-analyses, and prognostic charts, explicitly framed by the catalog as the foundation for correct and efficient use of modern computer analysis: a course built around verifying automated output, not merely producing forecasts. That framing is the binding constraint. Task-exposure research's jagged-frontier finding, that AI-assisted users are measurably less accurate with miscalibrated trust outside a model's competence, is precisely what this verification skill guards against. No general-studies designation locks the course structurally, but its stated role preparing meteorologists to use computer analysis correctly keeps it foundational within the sequence. At 24 months, computer-based diagnostic tools already exist, yet the human diagnostic literacy the course builds remains squarely necessary, holding the rating at Low.

By 2031, AI pattern-recognition on surface and upper-air data will handle far more raw map analysis, and capability-trend projections support fast growth in exactly this quantitative-analytical space. Yet the course's own rationale, training analysts to verify computer output, becomes more valuable rather than less as automated diagnostics proliferate: the jagged-frontier finding that users overtrust results outside a model's competence describes precisely the failure mode this training prevents. The prerequisite-substrate role caps erosion at 24 months but does not extend that specific protection through the five-year horizon, so the rating rises to Medium as raw execution automates while verification competence remains instrumentally load-bearing. The shift is from producing the analysis to checking it, a real but only partial erosion of instrumental need.

A decade out, capability-trend evidence suggests weather-data pattern classification will be thoroughly automated, and the base automatability of this course's descriptive analytical tasks rises accordingly. What resists erosion is the verification competence itself: diagnosing when an automated analysis is wrong requires exactly the manual technique this course teaches, and that oversight function persists even as first-pass execution does not. The rating holds at Medium rather than reaching High because this verification-oriented purpose is durable across the horizon, even under aggressive capability assumptions and continued diffusion of automated diagnostic tools into operational forecasting. The genuine uncertainty is how meteorology programs restructure the balance between hand analysis and automated-tool literacy by 2036, not whether some human capacity to check computer-generated weather analysis remains necessary; the central case still requires it.
MTR 3410.d: This is a course in interpretation, understanding, and analysis of weather data, focusing on conventional surface and upper- air data and use of these data in current weather diagnostics. Topics include traditional hand analysis of surface and upper-air weather maps, spatial and temporal cross-sections, thermodynamic diagrams, meso-analyses, and prognostic charts. These topics form the foundation for correct and efficient use of modern computer analysis. This is an essential course for operational and applied research meteorologists.

r: This course applies radar and satellite physics to interpreting meteorological products, with a lab built around reading imagery through computer display software, squarely an image-interpretation and pattern-classification task. Task-exposure research places quantitative, pattern-recognition-heavy analytical work among the more automatable categories, and remote-sensing image classification fits that profile naturally. The protective factor at 24 months is verification burden: distinguishing genuine storm signatures from ground clutter or sensor artifacts still requires trained meteorological judgment, and the jagged-frontier finding that misapplied trust degrades accuracy outside a model's competence zone is directly relevant to novice interpretation. No general-studies designation or accreditation mandate locks the course in place, and it is not itself prerequisite substrate for other required coursework in this sequence. With no structural cap beyond task and verification characteristics, the rating rests at Low.

By 2031, capability-trend projections point to substantially stronger automated storm and precipitation signature detection from radar and satellite feeds, and much of the routine imagery classification this lab teaches becomes AI-executed by default. Verification burden remains a meaningful brake at this horizon: false-alarm and missed-detection costs in severe-weather contexts keep a trained human check valuable, and the jagged-frontier miscalibration risk still applies to novel or ambiguous signatures. That protection is not absolute, however, and the rating rises to Medium as the underlying task shifts further into AI's competence. No institutional lock-in or foundational-scaffolding cap holds the rating down structurally at this horizon; the trajectory is driven mainly by task characteristics and a narrowing verification burden rather than by any external accreditation or transfer mandate.

A decade out, the central case has automated pattern recognition on radar and satellite products approaching high reliability for common signatures, consistent with rapid capability-trend growth in image-classification-adjacent tasks. By this horizon, the verification burden that protected the course at shorter horizons plausibly narrows further as false-positive rates on well-characterized phenomena decline, removing the main structural brake and pushing the rating to High. This is a genuinely uncertain projection: diffusion evidence shows AI adoption still lagging technical capability broadly, and rare or novel severe-weather signatures may keep demanding expert judgment longer than routine ones do. But absent a licensure or accreditation lock, and with no foundational role protecting the course, the central case points toward substantial automation of this specific interpretive task by 2036.
MTR 3420.d: This course provides a physics-based study of the uses of radar and satellites and their application to various meteorological problems. Basic theories of radar and satellites will be applied to the interpretation and analysis of various radar and satellite products. The lab component focuses on the interpretation of radar and satellite imagery using computer display software.

r: Atmospheric Thermodynamics applies the equation of state and the first and second laws to adiabatic processes, stability, and convection: rigorous quantitative problem-solving that underlies stability assessment throughout the meteorology sequence. Task-exposure research finds science and critical-thinking-intensive work comparatively protected even as quantitative execution is exposed, and this course sits at that boundary: AI can already solve thermodynamic-diagram problems, but the conceptual substrate students need for downstream coursework in dynamic and physical meteorology is not replaced by that capability. Verification burden is a real protective factor, since a mis-specified stability calculation propagates into severe-weather forecasting errors that are costly and not always obvious. No general-studies designation locks the course structurally; its protection instead comes from its foundational role and from the reasoning it demands. Rating Low at 24 months.

By 2031, AI systems will fluently execute thermodynamic-diagram analysis and stability calculations, consistent with capability-trend evidence on fast growth in structured quantitative-reasoning tasks. That erodes the work-the-problems-yourself rationale meaningfully. What resists erosion is the verification function: a wrong stability judgment in a convective-forecasting context is exactly the adversarial, non-obvious-failure scenario the jagged-frontier research warns about, and only a human who understands the underlying thermodynamics can catch the error before it propagates further into an operational forecasting decision. As foundational substrate for later meteorology coursework, the course's protective role holds the rating at Medium rather than allowing it to reach High; execution increasingly automates, but the conceptual and verification competence remains structurally necessary for the sequence built on top of it.

A decade out, thermodynamic problem-solving will likely be a solved computational task for AI systems under most capability trajectories, extending the execution erosion identified at the five-year horizon. The countervailing case is unchanged in kind though perhaps narrower in scope: this course's content remains prerequisite substrate for the physical and dynamic meteorology sequence, and diagnosing whether an automated stability or convective assessment is physically sound still calls on exactly the reasoning this course develops. The rating holds Medium, capped by foundational role rather than by task-exposure characteristics, which by 2036 favor high automatability. The open question is how thermodynamics is taught once computation is fully delegated, likely toward conceptual and verification emphasis, not whether the underlying competence remains instrumentally necessary for the curriculum.
MTR 3430.d: This course covers classical thermodynamics and its application to atmospheric processes. Main topics include the equation of state, first and second laws of thermodynamics, adiabatic processes of dry and moist air, stability, thermodynamic diagrams, thermodynamic variables, and convection.

No institutional lock-in or foundational role provides additional protection at this horizon. The genuine uncertainty is how thoroughly atmospheric-physics instruction shifts toward interpretive and evaluative work versus derivation, not whether some human physical-reasoning competence remains necessary for verifying automated output in this specialized subfield of the discipline.
MTR 3440.d: This course is an application of classical physics to common processes in the atmosphere. Main topics include cloud and precipitation physics, atmospheric radiation, radiative transfer, lightning, optical phenomena and weather modification.

r: Dynamic Meteorology derives and analyzes the conservation laws of mass, momentum, and energy governing middle-latitude synoptic-scale motion: the rigorous mathematical-physics core underlying essentially all forecasting theory in the discipline. Task-exposure research finds science and critical-thinking-intensive reasoning comparatively protected, and derivation-heavy theoretical work sits close to that core, since the pedagogical purpose is a student's own capacity to construct and evaluate governing-equation arguments, not merely to obtain a correct final answer that AI can already supply. As the theoretical substrate on which the discipline's forecasting and dynamics coursework depends, this is critical foundational scaffolding. No general-studies designation applies, but the foundational role alone caps the rating firmly. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this rigorous reasoning capacity is not eroded by AI's ability to produce derivations on request.

By 2031, AI systems will fluently derive and manipulate the governing equations this course teaches, and capability-trend evidence supports continued fast growth in symbolic mathematical-physics work. That does not reduce the instrumental need for a student to construct these derivations independently: this is foundational scaffolding for the entire meteorology theory sequence, and the jagged-frontier finding, that AI users are measurably less accurate and poorly calibrated outside a model's competence, applies acutely to fluid-dynamics derivations, where a plausible but wrong governing equation is dangerous and non-obvious. The rating stays Low, capped by foundational role regardless of how fluently AI can produce the mathematics; the course's task is building the reasoning capacity in the student, not merely generating the equations themselves for later use.

A decade out, AI mathematical-physics capability will very likely be strong by any reasonable capability-trend extrapolation, including for continuum-mechanics derivations of the kind this course covers. Even so, dynamic meteorology's core purpose, a student's own rigorous grasp of how conservation laws govern atmospheric motion, remains the substrate every later dynamics and forecasting-theory course in the discipline depends on, and that foundational role caps the rating at Low through 2036 in the central case. The wide uncertainty concerns how the course is taught alongside capable AI derivation tools, not whether foundational fluid-dynamics reasoning remains instrumentally necessary; task-exposure research's protection for critical-thinking-intensive work and the course's scaffolding role both point the same direction across the full ten-year horizon, even under an aggressive capability scenario.
MTR 3450.d: This course covers the fundamentals of fluid dynamics necessary for understanding large-scale atmospheric motions. The focus of the course is the development, derivation, and analysis of the laws of conservation of mass, momentum, and energy, as they apply to middle latitude, synoptic scale weather systems.

r: Hazardous Weather surveys the nature, causes, and predictability of hazardous weather events and the societal and economic strategies for protecting life and property: explanatory and risk-communication content built on an intro-level prerequisite plus a general-studies writing competency, rather than technical forecasting execution. This maps closely to interpreting information for others and evaluating compliance with protective standards, activities where AI already drafts competent explanatory and risk-communication text; observed-usage data confirms writing and office-style tasks are a prominent AI-use category. Neither institutional lock-in nor foundational scaffolding protects the course structurally at this horizon; it is a broad-elective survey, not a mandated or prerequisite course, so the rating rises to High as the explanatory and analytical content becomes substantially AI-deliverable. Diffusion evidence tempers the pace somewhat, since AI adoption across firms and institutions still lags the technical frontier considerably, but the course's own content characteristics point clearly toward high exposure regardless of how quickly adoption itself proceeds across agencies and the public sector.

A decade out, the central case has AI systems competently explaining hazard mechanisms, assessing predictability, and generating risk-communication material with little need for a student to independently master this content for instrumental purposes, consistent with capability-trend projections of continued rapid growth in exposed explanatory tasks. With no general-studies mandate, no accreditation lock, and no foundational role feeding required downstream coursework, nothing structurally protects the rating from reaching High. The genuine uncertainty is in how hazardous-weather education itself evolves, toward critically evaluating AI-generated hazard assessments rather than producing original ones, not in whether the current instrumental rationale for the course as currently taught persists through 2036; the accumulated capability and task-exposure evidence together point toward substantial continued erosion of that instrumental rationale over the decade.
MTR 3500.d: This course considers the nature and causes of hazardous weather, the predictability of hazardous weather events, and the economic and societal impacts of these events. The strategies for the protection of life and property from hazardous weather are also considered.

r: The internship places students in a supervised, on-the-job role at a meteorology-related company or agency under the auspices of an Earth and Atmospheric Sciences faculty member: an inherently workplace-embedded, mentored experience rather than a fixed content sequence. The verification and interpersonal-oversight structure built into the course, qualified supervision and faculty auspices, keeps the rating capped at Low even as the routine content of internship work shifts toward AI-assisted execution. The genuine uncertainty is which placements remain available and what interns actually do within them as AI reshapes entry-level meteorology work broadly; that is a labor-market question distinct from whether the supervised-experience course structure itself retains a genuine instrumental purpose for the student's professional development. MTR 3710.d: This course provides an on-the-job internship experience with a meteorology-related company or agency. The experience must be done under qualified supervision and the auspices of an Earth and Atmospheric Sciences faculty member. Internship requirements vary by department. For information and instructions on finding and enrolling in an internship, contact the Classroom to Career (C2) Hub at [contact omitted].

r: This field-based course combines classroom theory with direct field observation of severe weather across the Central and High Plains, including mandatory safety orientation and overnight travel for real-time storm tracking. A decade out, forecasting and nowcasting tools available to field observers will be considerably more capable under most capability-trend extrapolations, and remote-sensing coverage may reduce some exploratory driving, per diffusion evidence on growing but uneven AI adoption. Even so, the specific competence this course builds, a student's own embodied field judgment under real, hazardous, time-pressured conditions, is not a task an AI system performs on the student's behalf, and no realistic institutional or technological change removes the physical-presence requirement of severe-weather field training by 2036. The rating holds Low with high confidence; the honest caveat is that the tools informing field decisions will keep improving, while the instrumental need to develop hands-on field competence through direct embodied practice remains essentially unchanged.
MTR 3777.d: This field-based course is intended to combine classroom theories with actual field observations. Students are required to meet for an one-hour course on safety and expectations before the start of the class. The course will concentrate severe weather field observations across Central and High-Plains. Overnight stay will be necessary due to the ever-changing nature of weather patterns. Additional course fee is required. Students are responsible to pay for the outside incidentals, such as food and drinks.

r: Directed Study lets an upper-division student with a strong meteorology background pursue an individually chosen topic through frequent meetings with an instructor, under departmental permission: a mentored, topic-variable format rather than a fixed content sequence. MTR 3920.d: This course provides an opportunity for upper-division students with a strong background in meteorology to pursue study in a specific topic of interest and value. The course requires permission of the instructor and chair of the Earth and Atmospheric Sciences Department and frequent meetings between student and instructor.

r: MTR 4210 trains students to pull surface, upper-air, satellite, and radar data into forecasting software, then translate model output into a briefed forecast decision. Observed-usage data shows Computer and Mathematical activity already dominates AI use, and numerical-model guidance generation is largely automated in the underlying pipelines students learn to read. But the course's core deliverable is a spoken, real-time briefing under uncertainty, where a forecaster owns a decision with downstream safety consequences. That live, interpersonal, high-stakes judgment layer keeps verification burden high: a wrong call is costly and often not obviously wrong until afterward, so this lab's oversight still needs a human who understands the physical reasoning behind the forecast. At 24 months AI assists data assembly but has not displaced the trained judgment and briefing skill this course exists to build.

By five years, expect broader deployment of AI weather models, already competitive with numerical weather prediction on skill scores, into the display and analysis pipeline this lab teaches, compressing the data-gathering portion of the workflow further. Diffusion data suggests roughly one-fifth of firms use AI today, with weather-service adoption plausibly ahead of that average given how amenable gridded forecast data are to automated pattern-matching. Even so, the briefing and forecast-decision-making component, communicating confidence, caveats, and hazard implications to a human audience under time pressure, remains a verification-heavy, interpersonally embodied task AI performs less reliably outside routine conditions. The jagged-frontier finding that users misjudge AI accuracy on unfamiliar cases is directly relevant: a student who has not learned to independently evaluate model output is poorly positioned to catch AI's atypical-event failures. The rating stays protected but is less certain than at 24 months.

Ten years out, capability trends point toward AI systems handling more of the analytical chain this lab covers; task-time horizons for AI have been doubling roughly every four to seven months, which over a decade implies materially more capable systems for data synthesis and even routine briefing narration. It is plausible entry-level forecast-briefing tasks become largely AI-mediated, with a human reviewing rather than generating the product. Still, the course's function of teaching students to independently interpret raw data and defend a forecast decision under uncertainty addresses a verification role that persists even as automation depth increases, since someone accountable for the call must understand it. This produces a real but bounded rise in exposure: no confident prediction the underlying judgment skill becomes instrumentally unnecessary, only that more surrounding data-handling work is offloaded to automated tools by this horizon.
MTR 4210.d: This is a laboratory course in which the principles of synoptic meteorology and weather computer technology are used in developing a weather forecast. Students are introduced to computerized weather data access, display, and analysis using meteorological software applications. Students learn to use surface and upper-air data, satellite and radar imagery, numerical model output, and other weather data in the preparation of weather forecasts. Principles of weather briefing and forecast decision making are also introduced.

r: MTR 4400's core work, quasi-geostrophic diagnosis, computing vertical motion from omega-type relationships, tracking frontogenesis and jet-stream dynamics, is quantitative reasoning over gridded atmospheric data, closer to the mathematician and quantitative-analyst work task-exposure research flags among the most exposed occupations. As capability compounds along the documented trend of AI task-time horizons roughly doubling every several months, tools should handle more of the computational diagnosis end-to-end, from raw model output straight to interpreted synoptic structure, rather than merely assisting the calculus. Confidence is not absolute, since synoptic diagnosis of genuinely novel or extreme cases could still expose gaps, but the trajectory points toward substantial realized automation of this course's applied tasks.

A decade out, sustained capability growth of the kind documented in AI task-horizon and compute-scaling trends makes it plausible most of MTR 4400's diagnostic workload, computing vertical motion, tracing frontogenesis, characterizing cyclone evolution from data, is routinely AI-generated rather than hand- or human-computed, especially since these outputs check against well-defined physical relationships and so carry comparatively low verification burden. Nothing in the course's institutional profile, which carries no general-studies designation or licensure tie, offers durable protection against this. MTR 4400.d: This course is a calculus-based examination of the three-dimensional structure of mid-latitude, synoptic scale weather systems. Main topics include quasi-geostrophic theory, extratropical cyclone structure and evolution, diagnosis of vertical motions, jet streams, and frontogenesis. The lab component involves the hand analysis and computer-based analysis of live, forecasted, and archived weather data.

r: MTR 4410 has students derive the primitive equations, analyze operational numerical models, and write a finite-difference atmospheric model themselves, fundamentally a programming and applied-math exercise, the category task-exposure research most strongly associates with AI exposure, and consistent with the roughly 55.8% task-speed gains measured for AI coding assistance in controlled studies. Even so, building a correct, stable finite-difference scheme from primitive equations is exactly the kind of technically subtle work where the jagged-frontier finding applies: errors in numerical stability or boundary conditions are often not obvious without deep domain knowledge, so a novice relying on AI output risks the documented pattern of being less accurate while trusting the result more. That keeps verification burden meaningfully protective at 24 months, even though the underlying coding and derivation tasks are otherwise highly automatable and no institutional designation shields the course.

By five years, AI coding and mathematical-reasoning capability should meaningfully close the stability-and-correctness verification gap that protects this course today, particularly as models improve at checking numerical schemes against known physical constraints rather than only generating them. Given that programming tasks are already the most positively exposed category in task-exposure research, and given observed usage already concentrated in Computer and Mathematical work, it is plausible constructing and analyzing a finite-difference atmospheric model becomes a largely AI-mediated exercise by this horizon, with less need for a human to independently build the code from the primitive equations. The course carries no general-studies or accreditation lock-in to slow this. The main uncertainty is adoption pace rather than capability, since diffusion data show usage still uneven across sectors, but the applied-computing core of this course points toward high realized exposure by five years.

At ten years, sustained capability growth along the documented task-horizon and compute-scaling trends makes it plausible numerical model construction and finite-difference implementation, the applied core of MTR 4410, are routinely handled by AI systems with minimal need for a student to have built one by hand first. Verification burden, the main protective factor at shorter horizons, should erode further as models grow more reliable at catching their own numerical instabilities. No institutional designation constrains the course. This is nonetheless a long horizon: it remains possible genuinely novel modeling problems, or debugging failures in coupled systems, still call for the kind of foundational understanding of the primitive equations this course builds, so the projection should be read as a plausible trajectory under current trends rather than a confident forecast of obsolescence.
MTR 4410.d: This course presents the theoretical background to numerically modeling the atmosphere using the primitive equations. Current numerical models will be analyzed and finite-difference techniques will be applied to a simple computer model of the atmosphere developed during the course.

r: Mesometeorology asks students to forecast short-fuse, high-consequence hazards, tornadoes, flash floods, downslope windstorms, where a missed or false warning carries direct safety cost. Task-exposure research finds science- and critical-thinking-heavy work is negatively associated with AI exposure, and severe convective forecasting is a canonical example: outcomes are chaotic, lead times short, and failure modes non-obvious until damage occurs. That combination keeps verification burden low in the protective sense, meaning the oversight this task needs still requires a human who understands the underlying physical reasoning, not just AI output. Observed-usage data confirms AI adoption concentrates in office and computational tasks rather than this kind of real-time, high-stakes forecast judgment. At 24 months AI tools assist pattern recognition in radar and satellite data, but the decision-making and hazard-communication core this course builds remains substantially unautomated in deployed practice.

At five years, AI-assisted severe-weather pattern detection should be more capable and more broadly deployed, diffusion data already show meaningful firm-level AI adoption and that trend should continue, but mesoscale forecasting's defining difficulty is not pattern-matching alone; it is deciding, under genuine uncertainty and short lead time, whether to issue a warning with real consequences either way. That decision layer keeps verification burden protective: task-exposure research's finding that critical-thinking-heavy work resists exposure applies directly to short-fuse hazard forecasting, where an AI system operating outside its reliable range would, per the jagged-frontier finding, be trusted more than its accuracy warrants. No general-studies or accreditation designation offers additional institutional protection, but none is needed here, the task itself resists confident automation. The rating holds at low exposure, with more uncertainty than at 24 months about how far pattern-recognition assistance narrows the human role.

Ten years is long enough that capability trends, task-time horizons doubling every several months, compute scaling roughly fivefold annually, could meaningfully improve AI performance on convective-scale pattern recognition. But mesoscale forecasting's core challenge is a decision problem under irreducible short-term atmospheric chaos, not simply a data-processing problem, and the life-safety verification burden around issuing or withholding a warning is unlikely to disappear even if the supporting analysis becomes far more automated. Task-exposure research's association between critical-thinking-heavy work and lower exposure, combined with the absence of any documented breakthrough in reliably forecasting individual severe-convective events at the fine scale this course addresses, supports keeping this course's rating low even at ten years. This is the most uncertain of the three projections, and a discontinuous capability jump in short-fuse hazard prediction cannot be ruled out, but current evidence does not support assuming one.
MTR 4500.d: This is an advanced course in recognizing, understanding, and forecasting mesoscale weather events (severe thunderstorms, hailstorms, tornadoes, downslope windstorms, flash floods, snowstorms, etc.) with emphasis on theory, analysis of weather data, and forecast decision making.

r: MTR 4600 pairs research tasks AI already assists well, literature search, statistical analysis, technical-report drafting, where controlled studies show roughly 40% time savings alongside quality gains on professional writing, with a live oral defense of the work to faculty and peers. By five years, expect the literature-review, data-handling, and drafting portions of this capstone to be even more thoroughly AI-mediated, consistent with the trend toward higher realized automation in writing- and analysis-heavy work task-exposure research identifies as strongly exposed. The live oral defense remains a distinguishing, interpersonally embodied checkpoint, but as AI becomes normalized in the research workflow itself, the instrumental case for the course narrows toward that defense and the underlying research judgment a student must demonstrate, rather than the mechanics of literature search or statistical write-up, which increasingly happen with heavy AI assistance regardless of formal training. No institutional designation constrains this course. The projection carries real uncertainty, since how capstone programs adapt assessment to remain meaningful is partly a design choice rather than solely a capability question, but the writing-and-analysis core is trending toward substantial exposure.

At ten years, sustained capability growth suggests the research-support tasks in this capstone, literature synthesis, data handling, statistical analysis, even a first drafted report, could be routinely AI-generated with a student directing rather than performing the work, extending the trajectory already visible in professional-writing productivity studies and observed usage patterns. What should persist is the live, interpersonal defense component, since demonstrating independent understanding under real-time questioning is inherently embodied and resistant to full automation regardless of how capable the underlying research tools become. This produces a moderate rather than high exposure rating: real automation of the supporting research mechanics, but a durable verification role for the human defense that anchors the course's purpose. Ten-year capability forecasts carry substantial uncertainty, and how capstone assessment evolves in response is a program-design question this analysis cannot resolve with confidence.
MTR 4600.d: This is a capstone course required of all meteorology majors. Students engage in a research project that involves the application of scientific methodology to meteorological or climatological data and problem solving. Students learn to do literature searches, create a problem statement, handle data, perform statistical analysis, and present data and results. Technical writing and oral presentation skills are emphasized.
